exampleResponse: Public health messaging about diet must balance broad guidance with individual variation. The question of whether campaigns should actively promote plant-based eating or emphasize balance is worth exploring. While I see where Noah is coming from when he argues that individual needs vary based on genetics and health conditions, I would argue that clear, strong messaging can still include reasonable exceptions while guiding the general population toward proven benefits, since most people would gain from eating less meat. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Priya, who emphasizes that decisive messaging has driven successful behavior change in the past. For example, anti-smoking campaigns show that strong public health messages can shift population-wide habits far more effectively than vague, balanced guidance. Clear exceptions for documented medical needs still allow this broader guidance to remain both effective and fair.

subject: nutrition
prompt: We've been examining whether food companies should be required to reformulate processed foods to reduce added sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats, rather than simply relying on nutrition labels to inform consumers. Some argue that mandatory reformulation would improve public health more effectively than labeling alone, since many consumers don't carefully read labels or lack the knowledge to interpret them, meaning harmful ingredient levels remain widespread regardless of disclosure. Others believe reformulation mandates interfere too much with consumer choice and business innovation, and that improving nutrition literacy so people can use existing labels effectively respects individual freedom while still addressing health concerns. Should governments mandate food reformulation, or should they focus on improving nutrition literacy? Explain your reasoning.

classmates.name: Aisha
classmates.opinion: I support mandatory reformulation because relying solely on labels assumes an unrealistic level of consistent attention and nutritional knowledge from every consumer, which simply doesn't reflect how most people actually shop and eat. Countries that have required food companies to gradually reduce salt content in processed foods have seen measurable declines in population-wide blood pressure and related health issues, without consumers even needing to change their shopping habits at all. Reformulation addresses the problem at the source, protecting public health regardless of whether someone has the time or knowledge to carefully study every label.

classmates.name: Diego
classmates.opinion: I think improving nutrition literacy respects consumer freedom while still addressing health concerns, because mandatory reformulation removes the choice to buy products in their original form entirely, even for people who prefer them or have specific dietary needs that don't align with reduced sugar or salt. Teaching people to read and understand labels effectively empowers them to make their own informed decisions rather than having those decisions made for them by regulation. Companies should be encouraged, not forced, to reformulate, while public education ensures consumers can choose wisely regardless of what's available on store shelves.

exampleResponse: Improving public nutrition often requires choosing between mandates and consumer education. The question of whether governments should mandate food reformulation or focus on nutrition literacy is worth exploring. While I see where Diego is coming from when he argues that mandates remove consumer choice over original product formulations, I would argue that literacy alone cannot fix a problem rooted in daily shopping habits that most people don't have time to carefully manage, since reading every label consistently is unrealistic. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Aisha, who emphasizes that reformulation addresses the issue at its source regardless of individual attention. For example, countries that mandated gradual salt reduction saw population-wide health improvements without requiring any behavioral change from consumers at all. This approach protects public health broadly while still leaving room for individual dietary preferences and choices.

subject: agriculture
prompt: In our unit on farming practices, we've been debating whether governments should provide stronger subsidies to encourage the shift toward organic farming over conventional methods. Some argue that supporting organic farming through subsidies would reduce pesticide use, improve soil health, and lower the environmental impact of agriculture over time, since organic methods currently cost more and need financial support to compete with conventional farming. Others believe subsidizing organic farming could reduce overall crop yields at a time when global food demand is rising, arguing that conventional farming, especially when improved with precision technology, can feed more people while research into sustainable practices continues separately. Should governments subsidize the shift toward organic farming, or should support go toward improving conventional methods? Explain your reasoning.

classmates.name: Hana
classmates.opinion: I support subsidizing organic farming because the long-term environmental costs of conventional methods, including soil degradation and water pollution from pesticides, will eventually threaten food security far more than any short-term yield difference. Subsidies would help organic farmers compete on price while the industry develops more efficient techniques to close the yield gap over time. Healthy soil, free from years of chemical buildup, ultimately supports more sustainable long-term productivity than conventional methods that gradually deplete the very land future generations will depend on for food production.

classmates.name: Mateo
classmates.opinion: I think support should go toward improving conventional methods because organic farming currently produces meaningfully lower yields per acre, and with global population continuing to grow, we can't afford a widespread shift that reduces total food output. Precision agriculture technology, like targeted irrigation and reduced pesticide application guided by data, can address many environmental concerns without sacrificing the yields needed to feed a growing world. Investing subsidies into making conventional farming more sustainable reaches far more farmland and produces more food than funding a niche method that still struggles to match conventional productivity.

exampleResponse: Agricultural policy decisions often involve balancing environmental sustainability against immediate food production needs. The question of whether subsidies should support organic farming or conventional improvement is worth exploring. While I see where Mateo is coming from when he argues that conventional methods currently produce higher yields needed for a growing population, I would argue that ignoring long-term soil degradation risks far greater food security problems down the line, since depleted land eventually produces less regardless of the farming method used. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Hana, who emphasizes that healthy soil supports more sustainable productivity over time. For example, farmland managed organically for decades often shows better long-term resilience than conventionally farmed land that has gradually lost fertility from chemical dependence. Supporting this transition now helps ensure farmland remains productive and healthy for many future generations to come.

subject: agriculture
prompt: This week we've been examining whether genetically modified crops should be more widely adopted to address global food security. Some argue that genetically modified crops, engineered to resist pests, drought, and disease, are essential for feeding a growing global population, especially as climate change makes farming conditions increasingly unpredictable in many regions. Others believe that widespread adoption of genetically modified crops could reduce biodiversity, increase farmers' dependence on a small number of large seed companies, and that traditional crop breeding combined with better farming practices poses fewer long-term risks. Should genetically modified crops be more widely adopted, or should agriculture rely more on traditional breeding and farming practices? Explain your view.

classmates.name: Wei
classmates.opinion: I support wider adoption of genetically modified crops because climate change is making growing conditions far less predictable, and traditional breeding methods simply take too many years to develop the resilience farmers need right now. Crops engineered to resist drought or pests have already helped farmers in regions facing severe climate stress maintain stable harvests when conventional varieties would have failed entirely. With global population continuing to rise, we need every tool available, including genetic engineering, to ensure food security rather than relying solely on slower traditional methods that may not adapt quickly enough to rapidly changing conditions.

classmates.name: Fatima
classmates.opinion: I think agriculture should rely more on traditional breeding and diverse farming practices because widespread genetically modified crop adoption creates serious dependence on a handful of large seed companies who control patents on these seeds. This concentration of control can leave farmers, especially smaller ones, vulnerable to rising seed costs and legal restrictions on saving seeds for future planting. Traditional breeding combined with practices like crop rotation and diversified planting builds resilience without surrendering agricultural independence to a few corporations, while also better preserving the genetic diversity that protects against unpredictable future threats.

exampleResponse: Food security debates increasingly center on how to balance innovation with agricultural independence. The question of whether genetically modified crops should be more widely adopted is worth exploring. While I see where Fatima is coming from when she argues that dependence on seed companies threatens farmer independence, I would argue that the urgency of climate-related crop failures outweighs that risk, since traditional breeding often can't develop resilience fast enough to match how quickly conditions are changing. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Wei, who emphasizes that engineered drought-resistant crops have already saved harvests that would have otherwise failed. For example, farmers in increasingly drought-prone regions have maintained stable yields using modified crops when conventional varieties would have led to widespread crop failure. Careful regulation of seed patents could still protect farmer independence while allowing this technology to spread further.

subject: agriculture
prompt: In our discussion of farm labor, we've been debating whether agricultural work should be increasingly automated using robotic harvesters and AI-driven equipment. Some argue that automation is necessary to address chronic farm labor shortages and rising costs, allowing farms to remain productive and profitable even as fewer people choose agricultural work as a career. Others believe rapid automation would displace rural farm workers who depend on seasonal agricultural jobs for their livelihood, arguing that policies supporting fair wages and working conditions would keep people in these essential roles without eliminating jobs that entire communities rely on economically. Should agriculture move rapidly toward automation, or should policy focus on improving conditions for human farm labor? Explain your reasoning.

classmates.name: Ingrid
classmates.opinion: I think agriculture needs to move toward automation because labor shortages have already become a serious problem, with crops sometimes left unharvested because farms simply cannot find enough workers during critical seasonal windows. Robotic harvesters and AI-driven equipment can work consistently regardless of labor market fluctuations, ensuring food production remains stable even as fewer people pursue farm work as a career. Automation doesn't have to mean eliminating all jobs immediately, since it can address the specific gaps where labor shortages are most severe while human workers remain in roles requiring judgment and adaptability that machines still can't replicate.

classmates.name: Diego
classmates.opinion: I believe policy should focus on improving wages and conditions for farm workers because rural communities often depend heavily on seasonal agricultural jobs, and rapid automation would devastate local economies that have relied on this work for generations. Many workers choose to leave farm labor specifically because of poor pay and difficult conditions, not because the work itself is undesirable, meaning better policy could actually solve the labor shortage without needing to replace human workers with machines. Preserving these jobs while making them more sustainable protects both agricultural output and the livelihoods of entire rural communities that automation would otherwise leave behind.

exampleResponse: The future of farm labor raises real tension between efficiency and community livelihood. The question of whether agriculture should prioritize automation or improved labor conditions is worth exploring. While I see where Diego is coming from when he argues that better wages could solve labor shortages without displacing workers, I would argue that shortages are often severe enough that even improved conditions won't reliably fill every seasonal gap, since fewer people are entering farm work overall regardless of pay. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Ingrid, who emphasizes that automation can target the specific gaps where labor shortages are most severe. For example, a farm facing an unharvested crop due to a sudden lack of workers benefits directly from robotic harvesters that don't depend on an unpredictable seasonal labor supply.

subject: agriculture
prompt: We've been examining whether local, small-scale farming or large industrial farms are better positioned to sustainably meet future food demands. Some argue that supporting small, local farms builds more resilient food systems by reducing dependence on long supply chains, supporting biodiversity through varied crops, and strengthening local economies. Others believe large industrial farms are necessary because they achieve far greater efficiency and lower costs through economies of scale, making food more affordable and accessible, particularly for lower-income populations who would struggle with the higher prices typical of small-scale farming. Which model do you think should be prioritized for future food production: small-scale local farming or large industrial farming? Explain your position.

classmates.name: Amara
classmates.opinion: I support prioritizing small-scale local farming because the COVID-19 pandemic exposed just how fragile long global supply chains can be, with entire regions facing shortages when centralized industrial systems broke down. Local farms growing diverse crops build resilience against these disruptions while also supporting biodiversity that monoculture industrial farming tends to eliminate. Strengthening local food systems also keeps money circulating within communities rather than flowing to large corporations, creating more economically resilient regions that aren't entirely dependent on distant industrial production for their basic food needs.

classmates.name: Tomasz
classmates.opinion: I think large industrial farms need to remain the priority because their efficiency keeps food affordable for lower-income populations who would be disproportionately harmed by the higher prices typical of small-scale farming. Economies of scale allow industrial farms to produce food using significantly less labor and land per unit of output, which matters enormously as global population continues growing. While supply chain disruptions are a legitimate concern, the solution is strengthening and diversifying those supply chains rather than abandoning a model that has successfully kept food accessible and affordable for billions of people worldwide.

exampleResponse: Deciding how to structure future food production involves weighing resilience against affordability. The question of whether small-scale or industrial farming should be prioritized is worth exploring. While I see where Tomasz is coming from when he argues that industrial efficiency keeps food affordable for lower-income populations, I would argue that a food system too dependent on centralized production carries risks that outweigh short-term cost savings, since disruptions can leave entire regions without access at all. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Amara, who emphasizes that diverse local farming builds resilience against supply chain failures. For example, the shortages experienced during the pandemic showed how vulnerable heavily centralized industrial systems can be when disruptions occur. Strengthening these local networks alongside existing industrial capacity offers the most balanced path toward long-term food security.

subject: astronomy
prompt: In our unit on space exploration, we've been debating whether crewed missions to Mars should be a top priority for space agencies in the coming decades. Some argue that sending humans to Mars would drive enormous scientific and technological progress, inspire public interest in space exploration, and represent an essential step toward becoming a multi-planetary species that safeguards humanity against existential risks on Earth. Others believe the enormous cost and danger of crewed missions isn't justified when robotic missions can gather nearly identical scientific data far more safely and cheaply, arguing that funds would be better spent addressing pressing problems here on Earth. Should crewed missions to Mars be a top priority, or should space agencies focus on robotic exploration instead? Explain your reasoning.

classmates.name: Priya
classmates.opinion: I think crewed missions to Mars should be a priority because human explorers can make real-time decisions and adapt to unexpected discoveries in ways that robotic missions, limited by communication delays and preprogrammed instructions, simply cannot replicate. Historically, major crewed space achievements like the Apollo missions inspired massive public investment in science and engineering education that benefited society far beyond the mission itself. Becoming a multi-planetary species also provides a long-term safeguard for humanity against catastrophic risks on Earth, a goal robotic missions alone cannot meaningfully advance no matter how sophisticated they become.

classmates.name: Kwame
classmates.opinion: I believe robotic exploration should remain the priority because the cost and danger of sending humans to Mars is enormous compared to the marginal scientific benefit over what rovers and orbiters can already achieve. Robotic missions can operate for years without needing food, oxygen, or a return trip, gathering comparable data at a fraction of the cost and risk. With so many urgent problems here on Earth, like poverty and climate change, needing funding, it seems difficult to justify the massive expense of crewed missions when robotic technology continues improving and can accomplish most of the same scientific goals safely.

exampleResponse: Space exploration priorities often require weighing scientific ambition against practical cost and risk. The question of whether crewed Mars missions should be prioritized over robotic exploration is worth exploring. While I see where Kwame is coming from when he argues that robotic missions achieve similar results far more safely and cheaply, I would argue that human presence offers a kind of adaptability and inspiration that robotic missions cannot replicate, since real-time human judgment matters during unexpected scientific discoveries. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Priya, who emphasizes that crewed missions have historically driven massive public investment in science education. For example, the Apollo missions inspired a generation of engineers and scientists in a way no robotic mission has managed to match since. This kind of inspiration ultimately produces benefits that extend well beyond the immediate scientific goals of any single mission.

subject: astronomy
prompt: This week we've been discussing whether governments should significantly increase funding for searching for extraterrestrial life, including programs that scan the skies for signals from distant civilizations. Some argue that this research deserves substantially more funding because discovering evidence of life beyond Earth would be one of the most profound scientific achievements in human history, reshaping our understanding of biology, philosophy, and our place in the universe. Others believe the search consumes valuable resources with an extremely low probability of success, arguing that funding should instead prioritize research with more immediate, practical benefits like medical science or renewable energy technology. Should governments significantly increase funding for the search for extraterrestrial life? Why or why not?

classmates.name: Yuki
classmates.opinion: I think funding for this search deserves a significant increase because the potential discovery is so transformative that even a small probability of success justifies substantial investment. Understanding whether life exists elsewhere would fundamentally reshape science, philosophy, and how humanity views its place in the universe, a value that's difficult to quantify but genuinely profound. Additionally, the technology developed for detecting distant signals and analyzing exoplanet atmospheres often has valuable applications in other fields, meaning the investment produces meaningful scientific benefits even if extraterrestrial life is never actually found.

classmates.name: Lucas
classmates.opinion: I believe funding should instead prioritize research with clearer, immediate benefits like medical science or renewable energy, because the search for extraterrestrial life has an extremely low probability of yielding results within any reasonable timeframe. Given limited public research budgets, funding decisions should weigh probable outcomes against cost, and directing that money toward curing diseases or developing cleaner energy sources would help far more people in tangible, measurable ways. While the philosophical significance of finding alien life is undeniable, it shouldn't come at the expense of research addressing urgent problems affecting people today.

exampleResponse: Deciding how to allocate scientific research funding requires weighing profound possibilities against practical certainty. The question of whether governments should significantly increase funding for the search for extraterrestrial life is worth exploring. While I see where Lucas is coming from when he argues that limited budgets should prioritize research with clearer immediate benefits, I would argue that the potential significance of this discovery justifies steady investment even without guaranteed success, since the philosophical and scientific value would be immense. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Yuki, who emphasizes that the technology developed for this search often benefits other fields regardless of the outcome. For example, instruments built to detect distant signals or analyze exoplanet atmospheres have already advanced sensor technology used in entirely unrelated scientific applications.

subject: astronomy
prompt: In our discussion of space policy, we've been debating whether private companies should be allowed to lead major space exploration efforts, including missions to the Moon and Mars, rather than leaving this work primarily to government agencies. Some argue that private companies bring efficiency, innovation, and reduced costs that government agencies often struggle to achieve due to bureaucratic constraints, pointing to how private rockets have already dramatically lowered launch costs in recent years. Others believe space exploration should remain primarily government-led, since private companies are ultimately driven by profit rather than scientific goals, and important missions could be abandoned or shaped by commercial interests rather than the public good. Should private companies lead major space exploration efforts, or should this remain primarily a government responsibility? Explain your reasoning.

classmates.name: Elena
classmates.opinion: I think private companies should take a leading role in space exploration because they've already demonstrated remarkable efficiency, dramatically lowering launch costs through reusable rocket technology that government agencies took decades longer to even attempt. Competition between private companies drives faster innovation than a single government agency operating without that same competitive pressure, and lower costs ultimately mean more missions and scientific data for the same public investment. Government agencies can still set scientific priorities and safety standards while private companies handle the engineering and execution more efficiently and affordably.

classmates.name: Noah
classmates.opinion: I believe space exploration should remain primarily government-led because private companies answer to shareholders and profit margins rather than long-term scientific or public interest goals. A mission with no clear commercial return, like searching for signs of ancient microbial life on Mars, could easily be deprioritized or abandoned by a private company if it doesn't align with quarterly financial performance. Government agencies, despite their bureaucratic slowness, are accountable to the public and mandated to pursue scientific knowledge for its own sake, ensuring important missions continue even when they don't produce an immediate financial return.

exampleResponse: Space exploration policy increasingly involves deciding how much control to hand over to private industry. The question of whether private companies or government agencies should lead major missions is worth exploring. While I see where Noah is coming from when he argues that profit motives could sideline missions without commercial value, I would argue that clear government oversight of priorities can prevent that outcome while still benefiting from private efficiency, since the two approaches aren't mutually exclusive. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Elena, who emphasizes that private companies have already dramatically reduced launch costs through innovation. For example, reusable rocket technology developed by private companies has allowed far more missions to be funded within the same government space budget than before. Maintaining clear public oversight ensures scientific priorities stay protected even as private efficiency drives broader progress forward.

subject: astronomy
prompt: We've been examining the growing problem of space debris orbiting Earth and how it should be addressed. Some argue that international regulations should require satellite operators to actively remove defunct satellites and debris from orbit, even at significant cost, since the growing amount of debris increasingly threatens active satellites, space stations, and future missions with collision. Others believe strict removal mandates would be prohibitively expensive and technically difficult to enforce globally, and that resources would be better spent on improving tracking systems and collision-avoidance technology to manage the existing risk without forcing costly cleanup obligations on every operator. Should international regulations require active removal of space debris, or should focus remain on tracking and avoidance? Explain your position.

classmates.name: Sofia
classmates.opinion: I support mandatory debris removal regulations because the amount of debris in orbit is increasing at a pace that tracking and avoidance alone cannot keep up with indefinitely. Every collision between existing debris fragments creates thousands of new smaller pieces, a cascading problem that only gets worse the longer active removal is delayed. Requiring satellite operators to plan for end-of-life removal, similar to environmental regulations requiring cleanup of other kinds of waste, would prevent the problem from reaching a point where certain orbits become too dangerous and cluttered for any future missions to safely operate in.

classmates.name: Dmitri
classmates.opinion: I think focus should remain on tracking and collision-avoidance technology because mandatory removal regulations would be extremely expensive and nearly impossible to enforce consistently across every country and private company operating satellites. Many nations wouldn't cooperate with costly removal requirements, making a truly global mandate unrealistic in practice. Improving tracking systems and avoidance maneuvers addresses the immediate collision risk directly and affordably, buying time for removal technology to mature and become cheaper before attempting a large-scale international mandate that most operators currently can't reasonably afford to comply with.

exampleResponse: Space debris management raises real questions about balancing long-term prevention with practical enforcement. The question of whether international regulations should mandate active debris removal is worth exploring. While I see where Dmitri is coming from when he argues that global enforcement of removal mandates would be extremely difficult, I would argue that delaying action allows the debris problem to compound through repeated collisions, since each fragment creates more smaller pieces over time. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Sofia, who emphasizes that this cascading effect could eventually make certain orbits unusable for future missions. For example, requiring satellite operators to plan for end-of-life removal now could prevent the kind of runaway debris accumulation that would be far more costly and dangerous to address later. Acting now also spares future missions from inheriting a far more dangerous and costly orbital environment overall.

subject: art history
prompt: Many of the world's most visited museums display artifacts that were removed from their countries of origin during periods of colonial rule or military conquest. Some argue that these objects should be returned to their countries of origin as a matter of historical justice and cultural respect. Others argue that large international museums preserve these works safely, display them to millions of visitors from around the world, and tell a global story that would be lost if collections were broken up and sent back to their original locations. Considering the tension between historical restitution and universal access, should major museums repatriate contested artifacts, or should they keep them on display? Why?

classmates.name: Amara
classmates.opinion: I believe artifacts should be returned to their countries of origin whenever there is clear evidence they were taken through looting or coercion. Holding onto stolen objects perpetuates the power imbalance of colonial history, no matter how well the pieces are cared for. Communities that lost these artifacts often cannot fully understand or teach their own history without access to the physical objects. Modern shipping and conservation technology make safe transport possible, so the old argument that only Western museums can properly protect these treasures no longer holds up. Repatriation also builds trust and can lead to future collaboration, loans, and shared exhibitions between museums.

classmates.name: Dmitri
classmates.opinion: I disagree with returning every contested piece. Museums that hold vast encyclopedic collections let visitors compare art and artifacts from dozens of civilizations in a single afternoon, an experience that shapes how people understand world history as connected rather than isolated. If every country reclaimed everything taken from it, some national museums could lose the bulk of their collections, and many objects would end up in storage rather than on public display, since not every origin country currently has the facilities to exhibit them properly. Long-term loans seem like a better compromise than full repatriation in most cases.

exampleResponse: Museum collections rarely reflect a neutral history; they often reflect the outcomes of conquest and power. The question of whether contested artifacts should be repatriated or kept on display is worth examining. While I see where Dmitri is coming from when he argues that encyclopedic museums offer visitors a valuable comparative view of world history, I would argue that this convenience does not outweigh the harm of holding onto looted objects, since access to one's own heritage matters more than convenience for foreign visitors. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Amara, who emphasizes that modern conservation technology removes the old justification for keeping stolen artifacts abroad. For example, a museum could repatriate an artifact while negotiating a long-term loan agreement, satisfying both restitution and public access.

subject: art history
prompt: In many university art history programs, survey courses have traditionally centered on the European and North American canon, from ancient Greece through modern art movements. Some professors argue that this canon remains foundational and should still form the core of introductory courses, with non-Western art offered as separate electives. Others argue that survey courses should be restructured from the start to give equal weight to African, Asian, Latin American, and Indigenous traditions, rather than treating them as optional additions. Considering how the structure of a curriculum shapes students' sense of what counts as important art, should introductory art history courses keep the traditional Western-centered structure, or should they be redesigned to include non-Western traditions equally from the beginning? Why?

classmates.name: Kenji
classmates.opinion: I think the traditional Western canon should remain the backbone of an introductory course, mainly for practical reasons. Many technical concepts in art history, like perspective, chiaroscuro, and the development of oil painting, are traditionally taught through European examples, and students need a shared vocabulary before branching out. Once that foundation is set, students are better equipped to appreciate how other traditions developed their own distinct techniques and values. Electives focused on non-Western art then become richer experiences rather than rushed additions squeezed into a single overloaded semester.

classmates.name: Fatima
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because starting with only the Western canon quietly teaches students that European art is the default and everything else is supplementary. Techniques like perspective or shading exist in different forms across many cultures, and a course could just as easily introduce foundational concepts using Chinese landscape painting or West African sculpture. Restructuring the survey course to include multiple traditions from day one would give students a more accurate picture of art history as a global conversation rather than a single lineage with occasional side notes.

exampleResponse: The structure of an introductory course quietly signals to students what counts as central versus optional in a field. The question of whether art history surveys should keep their traditional Western focus or be redesigned around equal representation is worth examining. While I see where Kenji is coming from when he argues that a shared technical vocabulary makes early lessons easier to teach, I would argue that this vocabulary does not have to come only from European examples, since techniques like perspective and shading appear in many traditions. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Fatima, who emphasizes that treating non-Western art as supplementary shapes students' assumptions about what matters most. For example, a professor could open the semester comparing Renaissance and Chinese landscape techniques side by side.

subject: art history
prompt: Conservators who work on historic paintings and sculptures often face a difficult decision about how much restoration is appropriate. Some argue that damaged or faded artworks should be restored as closely as possible to their original appearance, using modern techniques to repair cracks, clean dulled colors, and reconstruct missing sections. Others argue that visible signs of age and past damage are part of an artwork's history and should be left largely untouched, since aggressive restoration can erase evidence of how the piece survived across centuries. Considering the risk of losing authentic history versus the appeal of seeing an artwork closer to its original state, should conservators fully restore damaged artworks, or should they preserve them with visible signs of age? Why?

classmates.name: Ingrid
classmates.opinion: I think artworks should be restored as close to their original condition as reasonably possible. Most artists created their work with specific colors, textures, and compositions in mind, and centuries of grime, fading, and cracking distort that original vision. When a painting is properly cleaned and restored, viewers can finally see details and colors the artist intended, rather than a muted, damaged version. Modern conservation techniques are precise enough to avoid harming the underlying material, so the fear of damaging the piece further is less relevant today than it was decades ago.

classmates.name: Santiago
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because an artwork's damage often tells its own story, showing where it traveled, what it survived, or how it was valued across generations. Removing every crack or stain in the name of restoring an 'original' vision assumes we can know with certainty what that original vision looked like, which is not always true. Aggressive restoration has, in some famous cases, permanently removed layers of original paint by mistake. Leaving visible signs of age respects the artwork's full history rather than just its first moment of creation.

exampleResponse: Deciding how to treat a damaged historic artwork involves balancing two different values: authenticity to the artist's original vision and honesty about the object's full history. The question of full restoration versus preserving visible age is worth examining. While I see where Ingrid is coming from when she argues that modern techniques can safely reveal an artist's intended colors, I would argue that certainty about the 'original' appearance is often overstated, since much of that information has been lost over time. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Santiago, who emphasizes that visible damage is itself part of an artwork's story. For example, a conservator could stabilize a painting to prevent further decay while leaving faded areas untouched rather than repainting them entirely.

subject: art history
prompt: Cities around the world are debating how to treat street art that appears on public walls without permission from property owners or city authorities. Some argue that this work should be recognized as a legitimate art form, protected from removal, and even funded through public art programs, since it can transform ordinary neighborhoods and give voice to artists who lack access to galleries. Others argue that unauthorized street art is a form of vandalism regardless of artistic quality, since it damages private property and its permanence depends entirely on the will of whoever created it rather than the consent of building owners. Considering these competing views on public space and property rights, should cities protect and preserve street art, or should they treat it as vandalism to be removed? Why?

classmates.name: Thandiwe
classmates.opinion: I think cities should protect street art rather than treat it as pure vandalism. Some of the most celebrated public art in the world started as unauthorized work on city walls, and removing it immediately would have erased pieces that later became sources of civic pride and tourism revenue. Street art also gives visibility to artists who cannot afford gallery space or formal training, allowing creative expression to reach people who might never visit a museum. Cities could set up review panels to identify pieces worth preserving rather than removing everything on sight.

classmates.name: Oskar
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because allowing unauthorized art on private property undermines the basic right of owners to decide what happens to their own buildings. If a business owner wakes up to an unwanted mural covering their storefront, the artistic merit of the piece does not change the fact that their property was altered without consent. Treating graffiti as automatically protected also creates confusion for property owners who want to repaint or renovate their buildings, since they may fear backlash for removing something labeled as art.

exampleResponse: Public walls occupy a strange middle ground between shared civic space and private property, which is exactly why this debate is worth examining. While I see where Oskar is coming from when he argues that unauthorized murals override an owner's right to control their own property, I would argue that outright removal ignores the cultural and community value some pieces develop over time, since not all street art is created equal. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Thandiwe, who emphasizes that many celebrated works began as unauthorized street art before being embraced by the public. For example, a city could require property owner consent going forward while still establishing a panel to evaluate and preserve exceptional existing pieces.

subject: music
prompt: Musicians and industry advocates have criticized streaming platforms for paying artists a very small fraction of a cent per stream, arguing that even popular songs generate little income unless they are played millions of times. Some argue that streaming services should restructure their payment models to give artists a significantly larger share of revenue, even if that means raising subscription prices for listeners. Others argue that keeping subscriptions affordable is essential for reducing piracy and expanding access to music, and that raising prices could shrink the paying user base, ultimately hurting artists more than it helps. Considering the tradeoff between fair artist compensation and affordable access for listeners, should streaming platforms raise prices to pay artists more, or should they keep prices low? Why?

classmates.name: Rafael
classmates.opinion: I think platforms should raise prices if that is what it takes to pay artists fairly. Musicians spend months or years creating an album, and receiving a fraction of a cent per stream does not reflect that effort, especially for smaller independent artists who do not have concert tours or merchandise sales to fall back on. Listeners already pay for coffee or streaming subscriptions without much complaint, so a modest price increase seems reasonable if it meaningfully improves how artists are compensated for their work. Fair pay could also encourage more people to pursue music professionally.

classmates.name: Yuki
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because raising prices risks pushing subscribers back toward piracy or free ad-supported tiers, which often pay artists even less. Affordability keeps the paying subscriber base large, and a bigger base spread across many royalty payments can end up generating more total revenue for artists than a smaller base paying higher fees. Instead of raising prices, platforms could restructure how the royalty pool is divided, giving proportionally more to smaller artists rather than concentrating payouts among a handful of global superstars who already earn well from touring.

exampleResponse: Streaming has reshaped how artists earn a living, and the question of how platforms should balance artist pay against listener affordability is worth examining. While I see where Yuki is coming from when she argues that higher prices could push listeners back toward piracy, I would argue that this risk is often exaggerated, since most listeners have grown used to paying for convenient, ad-free access. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Rafael, who emphasizes that current per-stream payments fail to reflect the time and effort artists invest in their work. For example, a platform could introduce a modest price increase paired with a transparent royalty model that directs more revenue toward independent musicians rather than established superstars.

subject: music
prompt: Music teachers disagree about how foundational music theory and notation should be in school music programs. Some argue that students should be required to learn to read and write standard music notation, since this skill allows them to study a huge range of written repertoire, communicate precisely with other musicians, and understand the structure behind the music they play. Others argue that requiring notation literacy can discourage students who learn best by ear or through improvisation, and that many successful musicians across genres like jazz, folk, and popular music developed strong skills without ever mastering formal notation. Considering these different paths to musical skill, should schools require students to learn traditional notation, or should they allow students to learn primarily by ear? Why?

classmates.name: Nadia
classmates.opinion: I think schools should require notation literacy because it gives students access to centuries of written music they could not otherwise learn. Without knowing how to read notation, a student cannot pick up a score for an orchestral piece, a choir arrangement, or even sheet music for a song they want to learn on their own. Notation also creates a shared language that allows musicians who have never met to rehearse and perform together immediately, since everyone can interpret the same written instructions the same way.

classmates.name: Kwame
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because requiring notation as the primary path can turn away talented students who naturally learn by listening and imitating. Many great musicians in jazz, blues, and folk traditions built their skills entirely through ear training and improvisation, developing a deep intuitive understanding of rhythm and harmony without ever needing sheet music. Forcing every student through the same notation-based curriculum risks discouraging students whose strengths lie elsewhere, when a more flexible program could nurture both kinds of musical learners instead of favoring one exclusively.

exampleResponse: Music education has to decide whether written notation is a universal requirement or just one path among several toward musical skill. This tension between structured literacy and ear-based learning is worth examining. While I see where Kwame is coming from when he argues that many great musicians in jazz and folk traditions never relied on notation, I would argue that notation still offers unmatched access to written repertoire that ear training alone cannot provide, since it opens doors to unfamiliar music. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Nadia, who emphasizes that shared notation lets musicians who have never met perform together seamlessly. For example, a program could teach basic notation while still setting aside time each week for ear-based improvisation exercises.

subject: music
prompt: Artificial intelligence tools can now generate original melodies, harmonies, and even full arrangements in seconds, raising new questions for the music industry. Some argue that AI-generated compositions should be eligible for the same awards, chart rankings, and royalties as music created entirely by human composers, since the final product is what listeners judge, regardless of how it was made. Others argue that music recognition systems exist specifically to celebrate human creativity, skill, and emotional expression, and that including AI-generated work in the same categories would devalue the effort and artistry involved in traditional composition. Considering how AI is changing what counts as musical creativity, should AI-generated music be eligible for the same recognition as human-composed music, or should it be treated separately? Why?

classmates.name: Selin
classmates.opinion: I think AI-generated music should be treated separately from human-composed music, at least for major recognition and awards. Music awards have traditionally celebrated not just the final sound but the years of training, personal experience, and emotional intention behind a piece. An AI model trained on existing songs does not experience heartbreak, joy, or the events that typically inspire human composers, so judging its output by the same standards blurs an important distinction that listeners and the industry have relied on for generations.

classmates.name: Milan
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because listeners generally cannot tell, and often do not care, whether a piece was composed by a human or generated by AI if the final result sounds compelling. If an award is meant to recognize quality and impact, then artificial origin should not automatically disqualify a composition, especially since AI tools are usually guided and edited by human musicians before release anyway. Creating a separate category could also stigmatize legitimate hybrid works that combine human creativity with AI-assisted tools.

exampleResponse: As AI composition tools become more capable, the music industry has to decide what standard actually defines award-worthy work. This question about whether AI-generated music deserves the same recognition as human compositions is worth examining. While I see where Milan is coming from when he argues that listeners often cannot distinguish AI-generated pieces from human ones, I would argue that recognition systems exist to honor more than sound quality alone, since they also celebrate the personal experience behind a piece. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Selin, who emphasizes that awards have long recognized the human effort and emotion behind composition. For example, award shows could create a separate category for AI-assisted work rather than blending it into traditional composition categories.

subject: music
prompt: Major concert tours today often feature elaborate stage designs, pyrotechnics, video screens, and choreographed visual effects alongside the music itself. Some argue that concerts should prioritize these visual elements, since audiences increasingly expect a full sensory experience and memorable spectacle is part of what makes a ticket price worth paying. Others argue that concerts should prioritize sound quality and live musicianship above all else, since the core reason people attend a concert is to hear music performed well, and elaborate productions can sometimes distract from or even mask weak vocal or instrumental performances. Considering these different priorities for what makes a concert successful, should performers focus primarily on visual spectacle, or should they prioritize musicianship and sound quality? Why?

classmates.name: Bilal
classmates.opinion: I think concerts should prioritize musicianship and sound quality above all else. People ultimately pay to hear an artist perform their songs well, and if the sound mixing is poor or the vocals are clearly not live, no amount of stage design can make up for that disappointment. Some of the most memorable concerts I have attended relied on minimal staging, just a well-rehearsed band and a great sound system, proving that visual spectacle is not necessary to create a powerful, unforgettable live experience for the audience.

classmates.name: Ines
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because modern audiences are paying premium prices for something beyond just hearing a song they can already stream at home in perfect quality. Visual spectacle turns a concert into a unique, one-time event, creating memories through stage design, lighting, and choreography that no recording can replicate. As long as the sound quality remains solid, adding spectacle enhances rather than replaces good musicianship, giving audiences a reason to choose a live show over listening to the studio album.

exampleResponse: Concerts today serve two goals at once, delivering music and creating a memorable visual experience, and audiences do not always agree on which one should come first. While I see where Ines is coming from when she argues that spectacle gives audiences something unique they cannot get from streaming at home, I would argue that spectacle only works if the musical foundation is already strong, since flashy staging cannot fix poor sound or weak vocals. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Bilal, who emphasizes that memorable concerts often rely on skilled performance rather than elaborate production. For example, a tour could invest in an excellent live sound system first and treat visual elements as a secondary enhancement rather than the main attraction.

subject: literature
prompt: Publishers occasionally face pressure to revise classic novels that contain racial slurs, outdated stereotypes, or language considered offensive by today's standards. Some argue that these books should be edited or annotated for modern readers, replacing or removing harmful language so that new generations can enjoy the story without being alienated or hurt by outdated terms. Others argue that classic texts should remain exactly as their authors wrote them, since altering the original language erases important historical context and can prevent readers from understanding the attitudes of the era in which the book was written. Considering the tension between accessibility and historical accuracy, should publishers edit classic literature for modern sensibilities, or preserve it in its original unedited form? Why?

classmates.name: Anika
classmates.opinion: I think classic texts should be preserved in their original form, with context provided through introductions or footnotes rather than edits to the actual text. Changing an author's original words, even offensive ones, distorts the historical record and can mislead readers into thinking attitudes from that era were less harsh than they actually were. Reading a text exactly as it was written, alongside historical context explaining why certain language was used, teaches students more about history than a sanitized version ever could.

classmates.name: Cyrus
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because the goal of publishing classic literature is to keep it relevant and readable for new generations, not to preserve every word as a museum artifact. If outdated slurs distract or alienate readers to the point where they stop reading altogether, then the deeper themes and lessons of the book never actually reach them. A carefully edited version, clearly marked as adapted, could sit alongside the original scholarly edition, giving casual readers an accessible option without eliminating the unedited text for researchers.

exampleResponse: Classic literature often carries language that reflects the biases of its time, forcing publishers to weigh historical accuracy against reader comfort. This debate over editing classic texts is worth examining. While I see where Cyrus is coming from when he argues that offensive language can alienate readers before they reach a book's deeper themes, I would argue that removing the original words sacrifices historical honesty for convenience, since readers deserve to understand the past as it actually was. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Anika, who emphasizes that footnotes and context can educate readers without altering an author's original words. For example, a publisher could keep the unedited text but add a scholarly introduction explaining the historical context behind difficult language.

subject: literature
prompt: English departments regularly debate what should guide the selection of novels for required reading lists. Some argue that literary merit, meaning strong writing craft, structural innovation, and lasting influence on the literary tradition, should be the primary factor in deciding what gets taught, regardless of a novel's moral messages or subject matter. Others argue that a novel's social impact and the values it promotes should weigh heavily in these decisions, since assigned reading shapes students' worldviews and schools have a responsibility to expose students to morally constructive stories. Considering these two different standards for evaluating literature, should reading lists prioritize literary merit above all else, or should moral and social impact carry significant weight? Why?

classmates.name: Wanjiru
classmates.opinion: I think literary merit should be the primary standard, because the purpose of a literature class is to teach students how language, structure, and narrative technique work, not to deliver moral instruction. Some of the most technically brilliant novels in history explore deeply flawed characters and disturbing themes, and studying them teaches students to think critically rather than simply absorb approved messages. If schools only assign novels with clearly positive morals, students miss out on learning from complex, ambiguous, and challenging works that push their thinking further.

classmates.name: Emil
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because required reading lists send a message about what a school values, and assigning a technically impressive novel that reinforces harmful stereotypes can do real damage to students who see themselves reflected poorly or not at all. Literary merit and positive social impact are not mutually exclusive; many technically excellent novels also handle difficult subjects thoughtfully and responsibly. Schools should be able to prioritize both craft and message when selecting required reading, rather than treating moral impact as an afterthought.

exampleResponse: Choosing a required reading list forces schools to decide what literature is actually for, whether that is teaching craft or shaping values. This tension between literary merit and social impact is worth examining. While I see where Wanjiru is coming from when she argues that ambiguous, challenging novels teach students to think critically rather than simply absorb approved messages, I would argue that ignoring social impact entirely risks assigning works that alienate or harm certain students, since required reading carries institutional weight. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Emil, who emphasizes that craft and positive impact are not mutually exclusive. For example, a department could select novels that are both technically excellent and thoughtful in how they handle difficult social themes.

subject: literature
prompt: Literary discussions frequently raise the question of whether a reader's knowledge of an author's personal controversies should affect how their work is read and taught. Some argue that a text should be evaluated independently of its author's personal life, since the work itself, once published, exists as its own object of study regardless of who wrote it or what they did outside their writing. Others argue that an author's actions and beliefs are impossible to fully separate from their writing, and that context about a controversial author can and should shape how a text is interpreted and whether it continues to be taught in classrooms. Considering these different approaches, should literature be judged independently of its author's personal life, or should an author's controversies factor into how their work is read? Why?

classmates.name: Greta
classmates.opinion: I think an author's personal controversies should factor into how we teach and interpret their work, especially in a classroom setting. Ignoring an author's harmful beliefs or actions can unintentionally endorse them, particularly when those beliefs quietly shape the themes or characters in their writing. Students benefit from understanding this context, since it teaches them to engage critically with a text rather than assuming the author's perspective is neutral or universal. This does not mean removing controversial authors from reading lists entirely, but rather discussing their context openly.

classmates.name: Rohan
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because a text takes on its own life once it is published, and judging its quality or meaning based on the author's personal failures distracts from analyzing the actual writing. Some of the most influential works in literary history were written by deeply flawed or controversial people, and refusing to separate the author from the text would mean excluding much of the literary canon. Readers can acknowledge an author's troubling history without letting it dictate how they interpret the words on the page.

exampleResponse: Literature rarely exists in a vacuum, which is why the relationship between an author's personal life and their work generates such disagreement. This question about separating text from author is worth examining. While I see where Rohan is coming from when he argues that excluding flawed authors would eliminate much of the literary canon, I would argue that acknowledging context does not require removing a work, since discussion and inclusion can coexist. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Greta, who emphasizes that ignoring an author's harmful beliefs can unintentionally endorse them in a classroom setting. For example, a teacher could assign a controversial author's novel while dedicating a class discussion to the surrounding context and its influence on the text.

subject: literature
prompt: Some literature teachers are experimenting with giving students significant choice over which novels they read for class credit, allowing them to select from a wide range of contemporary and diverse titles based on personal interest. Others maintain that all students should read the same required canonical texts, arguing that shared reading creates a common foundation for classroom discussion and ensures exposure to works considered essential to literary history. Supporters of choice argue that engagement and enjoyment increase dramatically when students read books that interest them personally, while supporters of a shared list argue that too much individual choice can result in students missing foundational texts referenced throughout academic and cultural life. Considering these tradeoffs between personal choice and shared cultural literacy, should literature classes let students choose their own novels, or require a common reading list? Why?

classmates.name: Anaya
classmates.opinion: I think students should have significant choice over what they read, because forcing disengaged students through a fixed canonical list often produces resentment rather than genuine appreciation for literature. When students choose books connected to their own interests or backgrounds, they read more carefully, participate more in discussions, and are more likely to continue reading for pleasure after the class ends. Teachers could still guide choices within a curated list of options, ensuring some structure while preserving the motivation that comes from personal investment in the material.

classmates.name: Anders
classmates.opinion: I disagree, because without a shared reading list, classroom discussions lose the common reference points that make deep literary analysis possible. If every student reads something different, teachers cannot lead detailed discussions comparing themes, symbolism, or structure across the group, and students miss out on debating the same text together. Canonical works are also referenced constantly in later academic study and cultural conversation, so skipping them in favor of personal choice could leave students at a disadvantage in future coursework.

exampleResponse: Deciding how much freedom to give students over their reading choices touches on both motivation and shared cultural knowledge. This tradeoff between individual choice and a common reading list is worth examining. While I see where Anders is coming from when he argues that shared texts allow for deeper group discussion and analysis, I would argue that forcing every student through the same fixed list can undermine genuine engagement, since disengaged readers rarely absorb a text's finer details. In this respect, I am inclined to agree with Anaya, who emphasizes that personal investment in a book leads to more active participation and lasting interest in reading. For example, a teacher could offer a curated shortlist of thematically connected novels, preserving both structure and choice.
